purpose: Lossless call wrapper for source-bound reuse; no new review occurred.

questions.question: Does the opening confuse persistent activity with an accurate value?
questions.answer: No. It asks how a useful quantity remains represented in changing activity and separates memory loss, eye-motion source and spatial firing arrangement.

questions.question: Are event, rate, tuning and anatomical roles distinguished correctly?
questions.answer: Yes. Spikes are events, rates are expectations, synapses transmit effects and a population pattern represents a coordinate. CA3 recurrence and input to CA1 are distinguished from CA1 output maps and entorhinal input.

questions.question: Does the pooling example use the right uncertainty and independence assumption?
questions.answer: Yes. A count has mean and variance r times duration. Twenty conditionally independent 20 Hz cells in 50 ms give mean count 20 and relative SD 1/sqrt(20), about 22.4%.

questions.question: Do covariance and MSD distinguish the stated physical and measurement effects?
questions.answer: Yes. Shared input contributes covariance, private noise changes individual variance, and MSD combines variance with squared mean. Neither statistic alone locates the responsible circuit.

questions.question: Does the chapter opening distinguish activity changes from memory changes?
questions.answer: Yes. Two disturbances can affect the population differently even when activity persists; the opening promises the two-cell example, accumulation and fixed-map comparison supplied below.

questions.question: Does the two-cell example have the claimed decaying and persistent directions?
questions.answer: Yes. The common deviation obeys dx/dt=-a x, while theta=(r1-r2)/(2k) has zero derivative.

questions.question: Do the variance, bias and shared-history calculations follow from their assumptions?
questions.answer: Yes. Independent zero-mean increments with variance 2D delta-t sum to variance 2Dt. Brownian motion is introduced as a continuous small-increment approximation.

questions.question: Is spatial randomness confused with changing spike noise?
questions.answer: No. A function drawn for a cell and environment remains fixed as the animal visits positions; actual spikes can differ across visits.

questions.question: Are the dynamical target and units consistent with the earlier foundation?
questions.answer: Yes. Theta is the initial value, theta is its later value, and barred rates denote deterministic steady states.

questions.question: Does the spike-to-rate model preserve event size, units and approximation scope?
questions.answer: Yes. A spike adds one to dimensionless activation s; weights change receiving input, phi converts input to a nonnegative rate and tau sets decay.

questions.question: Why does the left vector give the lasting coordinate change?
questions.answer: Differentiating the fixed-point family gives Ku=0. A left null vector normalized by v transpose u=1 removes decaying modes and extracts the lasting tangent displacement.

questions.question: Does noise projection give the scalar and multidimensional covariance formulas?
questions.answer: Yes. Left projection removes local deterministic flow; independent Brownian increments leave sum v_i squared r_i as the variance per time, equal to 2D.

questions.question: Is the symmetric formula and mutual-inhibition example correct?
questions.answer: Yes. Symmetry makes g prime a left null vector; normalization gives v_i=g_i prime/[tau sum r_j prime g_j prime], whose square belongs in the noise variance.

questions.question: Is local diffusion kept distinct from long-delay error?
questions.answer: Yes. The opening lists wrapping, boundaries, state-dependent spreading and systematic mean motion as reasons a local slope alone is insufficient.

questions.question: Do the density equation and excitation example follow from the stated stochastic model?
questions.answer: Yes. A zero-drift Ito increment has generator D F double-prime; the density equation differentiates Dp twice. Constant D gives Gaussian and wrapped-Gaussian solutions, with wrapped error tending to pi squared/3.

questions.question: Does the variance calculation incorrectly settle systematic drift?
questions.answer: No. Deterministic mistuning and possible noise-induced mean motion are separate from random spread. The convention comparison estimates a possible scale rather than the exact circuit drift.

questions.question: Do the figure explanations accurately distinguish simulation and readout claims?
questions.answer: Yes. Figure 1 defines the coordinate through noise-free return and separates displacement from readout uncertainty. Figure 2 tests diffusion in ring and mutual-inhibition networks, not animals.

questions.question: Does high information guarantee low diffusion in the opening?
questions.answer: No. It describes a lower bound for one network and explicitly says high information permits, but does not ensure, better stability.

questions.question: Is the information and inverse-error calculation valid for the stated observer?
questions.answer: Yes. Conditional Poisson counts give score sum (r prime/r)(n-rh), whose expected square is h sum r prime squared/r. Regular local unbiasedness and Cauchy Schwarz give variance at least 1/(Jh).

questions.question: Does the inequality and equality discussion survive the stated counterexample?
questions.answer: Yes. Cauchy Schwarz gives 2DJ at least tau^-2. Equality requires cellwise matching of retained-noise and information weights. An exponential transfer is sufficient for symmetric weights, but is not generally necessary.

questions.question: Are the parameter and width comparisons sufficiently controlled?
questions.answer: Yes. The text says what is held fixed and explicitly adds radial tuning and uniform centers before treating inverse matrix entries as reciprocal diagonal information.

questions.question: Does the opening separate the original value, cue state and later state?
questions.answer: Yes. Later spikes estimate the cue value and do not reveal the particular random displacements before it. T and L separately denote storage and observation.

questions.question: Why may storage and readout variances be added?
questions.answer: Zero conditional readout bias at every cue state and future noise independent of storage imply E[s e]=0. Translation invariance makes readout variance the same at each cue value.

questions.question: Does equal weighting give the stated variance and optimum?
questions.answer: Yes. Later state observations share earlier Brownian increments, so motion contributes a double covariance integral, not independent-state variances.

questions.question: Does backward precision accumulation produce the stated result and time interpretation?
questions.answer: Yes. Transporting a later likelihood backward adds transition variance; the new independent observation adds precision. The recursion gives P prime=J-2DP squared and P(0)=0.

questions.question: When does a fraction of spikes equal the same fraction of information?
questions.answer: Independent thinning with fixed probability alpha scales both rates and slopes by alpha, so observed J=alpha J while the full network D stays fixed.

questions.question: Do the two-time-constant and Gaussian-noise extensions preserve their assumptions?
questions.answer: Yes. Rate relaxation adds a second state block, while modeled spike noise enters only the synaptic block. Normalization gives tau+tau_m. Constant noise changes information weighting and makes a linear transfer sufficient for equality.

questions.question: Is the printed total-error lower bound correctly qualified?
questions.answer: Yes. From 2DJ at least tau^-2 follows sqrt(2D/J) at most 2D tau. Substituting this upper bound cannot establish the printed universal lower bound on total error.

questions.question: Does the Part opening fit the six chapters without overgeneralizing?
questions.answer: Yes. It scopes the result to a model circuit, distinguishes sustained activity from a changing angle and accurately maps the chapters to signals, diffusion, information and readout.
